newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bank of Spain seen giving private bonds new life.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Spain seen giving private bonds new life.

text.p: Bank of Spain plans to use private bonds and bills as collateral for its money market operations should provide a tonic for this weak market, analysts said on Wednesday.
Yet the central bank has not said whether it will launch repurchase agreements on bills, notes or matadors.
It has simply said it will use private paper as collateral in money market auctions -- a move which should reduce the expense of holding long bond positions.
"By boosting market liquidity, it should make holding these bonds cheaper," said Eduardo Augustin, chief dealer of non-government bonds at Bank of America in Madrid.
But much of the effect will depend on which kind of bonds are chosen for money market operations.

"If they do this on Matadors, they'll boost the market. Everyone will be more willing to keep peseta bonds in their portfolios even at a lower yield," said Luis Ordonez at Banco Santander de Negocios.
In recent months lower interest rates --improving corporate finances and making syndicated loans cheaper-- have reduced the amount of non-government issues.
Simultaneously new regional bonds have also been fewer because of the demands of European convergence criteria.
There are no official data on total domestic issues of private bonds and bills, but dealers agreed that Spain offers comparatively little in this respect.

"Other countries, say Germany or Great Britain, have a very wide range of private bonds and bills, with a good variety of risk ratings. This is not our case," said Isidro Blanch, money market director at Caja de Catalunya.
"Private issues are few, and often have short maturities. If we didn't have regional government paper we would have almost nothing," he added.
Overall Matador issues are expected to fall this year after almost tripling in 1996 versus 1995, reaching a volume equal to the three previous years put together.
The Matador primary market in 1996 saw new issues of 859.3 billion pesetas, up from 318 billion pesetas in 1995.
But private domestic bonds issues have been very slow so far this year.
"Issuers are not yet convinced yields have bottomed out. And we won't see a pick-up in activity since they won't admit prices have reached a peak," said Bank of America's Augustin.

At end-1996 Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo said one of the most complicated tasks in preparing Spain for forthcoming monetary union was to use private assets as collateral in money market operations.
He added that this year the Bank of Spain intends to start accepting high quality bills and notes with a high degree of liquidity as collateral.
"Although the global volume in these operations may be low, we intend to adapt current practices to the ones of the forthcoming European system of central banks," Rojo said.
